messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nalini was seventy-three, a widow of eight years, and had spent four decades building an interior design practice in the Chicago suburbs. She still took on the occasional small project—a living room re-upholstery, a kitchen backsplash—but she had stopped accepting new clients with offices in the downtown area. That was where it had happened, two years ago now, though the memory still felt more like a wound than a story she could tell.

It was late on a Tuesday evening in March. She had been leaving a client’s high-rise after finalizing fabric swatches for a dining room. The lobby was quiet. Two uniformed police officers were standing near the revolving doors. One of them—she could never recall his face, only the heavy navy blue of his coat—asked to see her identification. She fumbled for her wallet inside her handbag. The other officer stepped closer, and his hand brushed against her wrist as he took the bag from her. The texture of that rough wool sleeve against her skin was the detail that stayed, more vivid than anything else. She could not remember what she had said, or how many minutes passed before they handed her bag back and let her leave. There were gaps—a whole stretch of seconds, maybe a minute, that she had lost. Later, she tried to describe the scene to her daughter and found that the words would not come; she could only gesture at her wrist and say, “The fabric, the fabric.” The rest of the event came in disconnected pieces: a glint of a badge, the low hum of the fluorescent lights, the cold pressure of the officer’s hand on her elbow guiding her sideways. She knew she had done nothing wrong—she was a seventy-one-year-old interior designer carrying fabric samples—but the memory refused to assemble itself into a story that made sense.

In the months that followed, Nalini began to notice how often she encountered that rough wool texture. A new throw pillow in a client’s waiting room made her recoil. The sleeve of her own winter coat felt unbearable against her wrist. She took to wearing cardigans with soft cotton sleeves and avoiding any garment that used worsted wool. When she saw a police car parked near a coffee shop she used to frequent, her stomach dropped, and she found herself thinking, “Nothing good can happen anymore.” The sight of a uniform—even a security guard at the mall—triggered a wave of helplessness; she became convinced that she could not handle even the slightest upset, that her body was permanently on high alert and would betray her at any moment. Her body had become an enemy, trembling for no reason hours after a trigger had passed.

These appraisals looped back into her memory. When she tried to revisit the event in her mind, the gaps grew wider. She could not hold the sequence; she would start with the officers and then her thoughts would skid sideways to the texture, and she would feel the fabric against her skin again, and the sense that she was not safe. The more she believed she could not cope, the more fragmented the memory became. And the more fragmented the memory, the more sensitive she grew to triggers. A glimpse of a police cruiser on her street sent her heart racing; the touch of her own rough-knitted scarf made her jump. She had come to believe that even when she was safe, her body kept reacting as if she were still in danger, and that meant something was fundamentally broken inside her. Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her — and her attention snagged on these signals even when she knew, rationally, that nothing was out of place.

Nalini stopped working with clients whose offices were in buildings with security guards. She changed her route to the grocery store to avoid a corner where she had once seen a police car parked. She stopped meeting her old friends for lunch if the restaurant was near the downtown area. Her daughter noticed and began driving her to appointments, but Nalini felt a deep shame about needing help—she was supposed to be competent, independent. At night, lying alone in the house she had decorated herself, she would run her hand over the soft velvet of her bedspread and remember the roughness, and the gaps would yawn open, and she would whisper to herself, “I can’t do this.”

What finally made her pick up the phone was a new client inquiry—a young couple who wanted her to design their entire first floor. It was a beautiful project, high-end, local. But the address was two blocks from where the event had occurred. She could not even bring herself to type a reply. She sat at her desk, stared at the street name, and felt a wave of dread so physical that she thought she might vomit. For the first time she admitted that she was not simply getting older or becoming cautious; something was holding her captive. She told her daughter she needed to talk to someone, and her daughter found a therapist who specialized in trauma. Nalini is afraid of what she will find if she starts remembering more clearly—she suspects that the gaps are protecting her from something unbearable. But she is also tired of shrinking her life. What she hopes for, though she cannot quite say it, is that a single memory might finally stop hurting so much.
